metaData.originalTitle: 拉勾破产：一段互联网创业简史
metaData.title: Lagou Bankruptcy: A Brief History of Internet Entrepreneurship
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: Using Lagou's bankruptcy as a clue, this article deeply reviews its complete journey from incubation at 3W Coffee, rising during the mass entrepreneurship era, being acquired by a giant, failing to transform into education, and finally being forgotten by the AI era, marking the end of the era of universal wealth creation through the internet.
metaData.summary: Taking Lagou's voluntary bankruptcy application in 2026 as the starting point, this article systematically reviews the complete lifecycle of this vertical recruitment platform from birth to demise. The author closely ties Lagou's fate to the rise and fall of China's mobile internet entrepreneurship: launched in 2013, it took off relying on the network of acquaintances at 3W Coffee and the internet entrepreneurship boom; it became an industry star in 2015 thanks to the mass entrepreneurship policy; it sold 60% of its equity to 51job in 2017, losing its independence; after 2018, it attempted an education transformation as a second growth curve, but encountered internet layoffs and the collapse of the education and training industry; ultimately, it was forgotten in the AI recruitment era. Through Lagou's case, the article profoundly analyzes the vulnerability of vertical platforms within industry cycles—when the internet industry shifted from expansion to contraction, the myth of "programmers getting salary increases by switching jobs" that Lagou relied on also collapsed. The article also compares BOSS Zhipin, which rose during the same period, pointing out that Lagou's failure was not only a result of business competition but also the end of the era narrative represented by the "internet career advancement channel."

mainPoints.point: Lagou's rise and fall are highly synchronized with the mobile internet entrepreneurship cycle.
mainPoints.explanation: Launched in 2013, Lagou caught the wave of the internet entrepreneurship boom; the 2015 mass entrepreneurship policy pushed it to its peak; after 2021, internet layoffs and the collapse of the education and training sector led to the shrinkage of its core market. It almost perfectly replicated every step of China's mobile internet journey from excitement to fatigue.

mainPoints.point: The vulnerability of vertical platforms lies in their deep dependence on the host industry.
mainPoints.explanation: Lagou's success relied on the frantic expansion of internet companies and the myth of programmers switching jobs for higher pay. When the industry cycle reversed and employers stopped hiring, Lagou's business model lost its foundation, and its brand recognition became a liability.

mainPoints.point: Lagou's education transformation reflects a collective industry illusion.
mainPoints.explanation: Lagou misinterpreted the naturally occurring career advancement during the internet's high-salary expansion period as a service capability the platform could sustainably create. When the industry contracted, training courses shifted from investment goods to consumer goods, causing the second growth curve to collapse.

mainPoints.point: Lagou's demise marks the end of the era of universal wealth creation through the internet.
mainPoints.explanation: Lagou once sold the belief that "the internet industry needs more people," while the AI era's talent demand is more concentrated and picky. Moreover, its co-founder Ma Delong's new project, Lobstaff, has shifted to "recruiting digital employees," suggesting that companies may no longer need as many people.

keyQuotes: Lagou wasn't killed by a specific enemy. It simply outlived the world it depended on.
Lagou once sold the belief that 'the internet industry needs more people.' Lobstaff sells the future where 'companies may not need that many people.'
Lagou wasn't built from scratch. It was a commercial plugin incubated from the circle of acquaintances at 3W Coffee.
A recruitment platform doesn't record a person's value. It records the price the market is willing to pay for that person at a given moment.
What disappeared was the illusion Lagou once sold: as long as you stand with the internet, the era will give you a raise.

relatedArticles.title: How to Boost Efficiency with AI Without Burning Out Your Brain?
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article explores how to avoid cognitive decline caused by over-reliance on AI tools in an increasingly AI-driven world, offering specific suggestions such as thinking before asking, actively paraphrasing, writing before using AI, and embracing boredom.

relatedArticles.title: AI Cannot Eliminate Bureaucracy, and Flat Organizations Are Far from a Corporate Panacea
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: By analyzing organizational change cases from well-known companies such as Zappos, Medium, Valve, GitHub, Spotify, and Haier, this article argues that AI cannot eliminate bureaucracy, flat organizations are not a universal cure-all, and the core of organizational issues lies in the distribution of power, responsibility, and interests, rather than mere information transmission.

relatedArticles.title: China's AI: Perhaps Replaying the Script of Toyota's Detroit Upset
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: After visiting 14 AI labs in China, a US AI practitioner notes that chip export controls have not only failed to halt China's AI development but have instead fostered a competitiveness rooted in extreme efficiency, with China's AI building a unique efficiency moat under resource constraints, much like Toyota did in its time.

relatedArticles.title: Must 'Token' Die?
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article delves into the structural ceiling of token-based autoregressive large language models and introduces recent research, such as He Kaiming's team's ELF and ByteDance's Cola DLM, which shift the core computation of language generation into continuous space, signaling a potential paradigm shift in AI.

relatedArticles.title: How to Build an AI-Native Company?
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article is a translation of Anthropic's founder playbook, systematically outlining the core principles, common pitfalls, and specific applications of Claude products across four stages of an AI-native startup: Idea, MVP, Launch, and Scale.
